newsitem.title: UK: UK PSBR limits scope for pre-election tax cuts.
newsitem.headline: UK PSBR limits scope for pre-election tax cuts.

text.p: A higher-than-expected UK public sector deficit in August has cast doubt on the government's deficit target for the year and will cramp the scope for pre-election tax cuts, analysts said.
"We think the PSBR will overshoot its target," said Andrew Cates, UK economist at UBS. "Ex-privatisation proceeds, there's hardly any improvement in the cumulative total so far."
August's public sector borrowing requirement totalled 4.53 billion stg and that shortfall was flattered by privatisation proceeds of 436 million stg.
Economists had been forecast a PSBR of around 4.1 billion.
Excluding privatisation proceeds, the cumulative deficit for the first five months of the financial year totalled 16.1 billion stg. At the same stage last year, the deficit was 16.7 billion.

Add all that up and the government's PSBR target of 27 billion stg for 1996/97 looks ever more elusive and will make it tougher for Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke to conjure up substantial, vote-winning tax cuts in his November budget.
"I don't think Clarke can give too much away," Cates said.

But few analysts thought the state of Britain's public finances would preclude tax cuts altogether. Clarke will come under intense pressure from his ruling Conservative Party to do whatever he can to boost their chances of re-election.
The election must be held by May 1997 and the Conservatives continue to lag the opposition Labour Party in the polls.
Cates said Clarke will produce tax cuts of around three billion stg but match them with offsetting spending cuts.
Jeremy Hawkins, senior economic adviser at BankAmerica, agreed it was too early to rule out tax cuts.
"But another poor set of (PSBR) figures this month would clearly add to the pressure for rates to be lowered instead."
Tuesday's PSBR figure suggested that July's public sector repayment of 1.66 billion stg, boosted by a flood of corporation tax receipts, may have been a flash in the pan.
"Today's data fit in with the idea that the larger than forecast debt repayment in July was erratic and, at least in part, a function of changes to the timing of tax receipts," Hawkins said.
If there was any silver lining for Clarke in Tuesday's figures it was that government spending was reined in a little.
"Government spending came in slightly better than expected," said Ciaran Barr, UK economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell. "All the damage this month was on the receipts side, particularly VAT."
Value added tax receipts totalled 3.294 billion stg in August, well down on July's haul of 4.543 billion.
Barr thought the government's PSBR target could be met but conceded the August figures were disappointing.
Cates said there were problems on both sides of the equation. "Revenues are undershooting and expenditure is slightly overshooting," he said.
